Empirical Research Plan – Impact of Islamic‐Party Victories in Turkey’s 1994 Municipal Elections
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1. Identification Strategy
   • Primary design: Sharp Regression-Discontinuity Design (RDD) around the 0-vote-margin cutoff in the 1994 municipal elections.  
   • Augmentation: Difference-in-Discontinuities (DiD-RD) / event-study panel to trace dynamics before and after 1994 and to net out any pre-existing discontinuities.  
   Rationale: In each municipality the Islamic party either barely won or barely lost. Close races approximate random assignment, satisfying the core RD assumption that potential outcomes are smooth through the 0-margin cutoff. The available panel of pre- and post-election outcomes lets us (i) improve precision, (ii) test for pre-trends, and (iii) explore medium-run effects.

2. Treatment and Control
   • Treatment indicator Ti : 1 if Islamic-party mayor elected in 1994; 0 otherwise.  
   • Running variable Ri : Islamic party’s victory margin = (% Islamic votes – % runner-up votes).  
   • Cutoff c = 0. Municipalities with Ri ≥ 0 are treated; Ri < 0 are controls.  
   • Timing: Treatment starts January 1995 (installation of the new mayor) and lasts until the next local election (1999). Observed outcomes are indexed by year t ∈ {1991,…,2001}.  
   • Estimation sample: |Ri| ≤ h where h is the optimal Imbens–Kalyanaraman (IK) or Calonico–Cattaneo–Titiunik (CCT) bandwidth.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions
   A1. Continuity: In the absence of treatment, potential outcomes evolve smoothly in Ri at c=0. Plausible because a few hundred votes either way rarely reflect meaningful differences in fundamentals.  
   A2. No manipulation of Ri: Parties could not precisely sort around 0. Turkey used paper ballots, single-round, same-day count; ballot stuffing sophisticated enough to target an exact margin is unlikely. We will test via McCrary density and covariate balance.  
   A3. Stable composition / SUTVA: Municipalities are the correct, non-interacting units. Some spillovers (e.g., migration to Islamic cities) are possible but likely second-order over a 4-year term.  
   A4. Consistent timing: All treated units receive the “dose” at the same calendar date; control units never receive it in the window. 1994 was the only local election in that window.

4. Threats to Identification and Remedies
   Threat 1 – Sorting or fraud near cutoff  
      • McCrary density test; heaping tests at specific margins  
      • Covariate RD plots (population, education, GDPpc) to confirm smoothness  
   Threat 2 – Differential trends predating 1994, e.g., Islamic vote share reflects latent growth patterns  
      • Difference-in-Discontinuities: estimate ΔY = (Ypost − Ypre) and run RD on changes  
      • Include municipality fixed effects and pre-trend controls in an event-study RD panel  
   Threat 3 – Spillovers / general equilibrium (e.g., neighbouring towns)  
      • Spatial lag controls; exclude neighbours within 20 km in robustness  
      • Cluster standard errors at sub-provincial level and re-estimate on non-contiguous subsamples

5. R Code Outline
```r
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)      # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)          # panel & FE regressions
library(rdrobust)        # RD estimation
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load data
d <- fread("turkey_municipal_panel.csv")   # one row per muni-year

# 2. Variable construction
d[, margin94  := islam_vote_share94 - runnerup_vote_share94]   # running var
d[, treat94   := as.integer(margin94 >= 0)]                    # treatment
d[, post      := as.integer(year >= 1995 & year <= 1999)]      # treatment window
d[, outcome1  := log(real_income_per_capita)]                  # example outcome
d[, delta_out := outcome1 - shift(outcome1, n=1, type="lag"), by = muni_id]

# 3. Sharp RD (cross-section, 1995 outcome)
cross <- d[year == 1996]   # first full fiscal year
rd_out <- rdrobust(cross$outcome1, cross$margin94,
                   p=1, vce="HC1", kernel="triangular")
print(rd_out)

# 4. Difference-in-Discontinuities (change 1996 − 1993)
pre  <- d[year == 1993, .(muni_id, outcome1_pre = outcome1)]
post <- d[year == 1996, .(muni_id, outcome1_post = outcome1)]
dd   <- merge(pre, post, by="muni_id")
dd[, diff := outcome1_post - outcome1_pre]
rd_diff <- rdrobust(dd$diff, d[year==1996]$margin94,
                    p=1, vce="HC1")
print(rd_diff)

# 5. Panel event-study within optimal bandwidth
h <- rd_out$bws[1]   # left bandwidth
panel <- d[abs(margin94) <= h]
fe_mod <- feols(outcome1 ~ treat94*post | muni_id + year,
                data = panel, cluster = ~muni_id)
summary(fe_mod)

# 6. Robustness: alternative bandwidth (±2.5%)
rd_alt <- rdrobust(cross$outcome1, cross$margin94,
                   h=0.025, p=2)
print(rd_alt)
```

6. Expected Results
Theory and prior qualitative evidence predict:  
   • Economic dimension: Islamic parties emphasised redistributive social aid and informal welfare networks. Expect a modest but positive increase (≈ 2–4 percent) in real income or poverty alleviation metrics for the bottom quintile relative to control municipalities.  
   • Social empowerment: Increase in religious schooling enrollment, mosque attendance proxies, and female Islamic dress prevalence (if measured). Direction: positive. Magnitude harder to benchmark, but 0.2–0.3 SD in standardized indices seems plausible.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RDD)
C1: No sorting/manipulation at cutoff  … 0.8  
C2: Smooth baseline covariates at cutoff … 1.0  
C3: Correct functional-form / bandwidth choice … 0.9  
C4: No other discontinuities coinciding with cutoff … 0.8  
C5: Robustness to alternative windows & placebo cutoffs … 0.9  

Average ≈ 0.88 → design appears strong but still contingent on passing empirical diagnostics.
